questions.q: State the Law of Demand and give one example of it from daily life.
questions.a: The Law of Demand says that when the price of a product rises, the quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises; price and quantity demanded have an inverse relationship. Example: when the price of tomatoes falls from Rs 60 to Rs 30 a kg, a family buys 2 kg instead of 1 kg (any suitable example).
s: States the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded
Gives a suitable daily-life example in which a lower price brings a larger quantity bought (or a higher price a smaller one)

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: Kabir notices that a sports shop sold more cricket bats in April, when the price was Rs 1,200, than in January, when the price was Rs 1,000. He says, 'This proves the Law of Demand is wrong.' Examine his claim.
questions.a: Kabir is wrong. The Law of Demand compares quantities at different prices only when other factors such as income, taste and season stay the same. Between January and April another factor changed: April brings summer holidays and the cricket season, so demand for bats rose even at the higher price (seasonality). So the higher sales come from a change in other factors, not from a failure of the law; at any one time, a lower price would still sell more bats than a higher one.
s: Says the law holds only when other factors are kept constant
Identifies a changed factor, such as the cricket season or summer holidays (seasonality), that raised demand in April
Concludes that the data do not disprove the law, since the two months differ in more than price

questions.q: Three households in a housing society buy ice-cream cones from a cart each week. At Rs 40 a cone they buy 2, 1 and 3 cones; at Rs 30 they buy 3, 2 and 4; at Rs 20 they buy 5, 4 and 6. (a) Find the market demand at each price. (b) When the price falls from Rs 40 to Rs 20, by how much does the market demand rise, and by how much does the second household's demand rise? (c) Using (b), say which curve is flatter, the market curve or the second household's curve, and why. (d) A fourth household with exactly the same demand as the first one joins the society. Find the new market demand at Rs 20.
questions.a: (a) Rs 40: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 cones; Rs 30: 3 + 2 + 4 = 9 cones; Rs 20: 5 + 4 + 6 = 15 cones. (b) Market demand rises by 15 - 6 = 9 cones; the second household's rises by 4 - 1 = 3 cones. (c) The market curve is flatter, because it adds many buyers, so the same price fall gives a larger rise in total quantity. (d) 15 + 5 = 20 cones.
s: (a) Market demand 6, 9 and 15 cones at Rs 40, Rs 30 and Rs 20
(b) Rise of 9 cones in the market and 3 cones for the second household
(c) Market curve is flatter because it adds the responses of many buyers
(d) New market demand at Rs 20 is 20 cones

questions.q: Ritu surveys a juice stall for a week. At Rs 30 a glass it sells 40 glasses a day; at Rs 25, 55 glasses; at Rs 20, 70 glasses; at Rs 15, 85 glasses. (i) What name does the chapter give to such a table of prices and quantities? (ii) Show from the data that the stall's sales obey the Law of Demand. (iii) The owner wants to sell at least 60 glasses a day. At which of these prices can he do so? (iv) Work out the money he takes in each day at Rs 20 and at Rs 15. (v) The owner says, 'The lowest price, Rs 15, will always bring me the most money.' Evaluate his claim using your answer to (iv).
questions.a: (i) A demand schedule (here a market demand schedule for the stall). (ii) Each fall of Rs 5 in price raises sales by 15 glasses (40, 55, 70, 85), so price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, the inverse relationship of the Law of Demand. (iii) Rs 20 (70 glasses) and Rs 15 (85 glasses). (iv) At Rs 20: 20 x 70 = Rs 1,400; at Rs 15: 15 x 85 = Rs 1,275. (v) The claim is wrong: Rs 15 sells the most glasses but brings in Rs 125 less than Rs 20. A lower price raises the quantity sold, but the money taken in also depends on the price of each glass, so the lowest price does not always earn the most.
s: (i) Names it a demand schedule
(ii) Shows that as price falls quantity rises, the inverse relationship
(iii) Picks Rs 20 and Rs 15
(iv) Rs 1,400 at Rs 20 and Rs 1,275 at Rs 15
(v) Rejects the claim: Rs 15 sells more but earns Rs 125 less, since takings depend on price as well as quantity

questions.q: Name the factor affecting demand in each case. (a) Families buy umbrellas and raincoats as the monsoon begins. (b) A family's income rises and it starts buying a costlier, better-quality brand of rice. (c) People rush to buy gold today because they expect its price to rise next month.
questions.a: (a) Seasonality: demand changes with the weather at that time of year. (b) Income of the consumer: a higher income lets people buy more or choose higher-quality products. (c) Future price expectations: expecting a rise, people buy immediately, increasing present demand.
s: (a) Seasonality (weather)
(b) Income of the consumer
(c) Future price expectations

questions.q: True or False: If the price of LPG cylinders stays the same while induction cooktops become much costlier, the demand for LPG cylinders will fall. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. LPG and induction cooktops are substitute goods for cooking; when one becomes costlier, people tend to switch to the relatively cheaper alternative, so the demand for LPG cylinders will rise, not fall.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: they are substitutes, so a dearer cooktop raises the demand for LPG

questions.q: For each change below, name the factor affecting demand and say whether the demand for the good named rises or falls. (i) A mother's salary increases; demand for good-quality school shoes in her family. (ii) The price of tea rises sharply; demand for coffee. (iii) The price of petrol rises sharply; demand for motorcycles. (iv) A family expects television prices to fall in the Diwali sale next month; its demand for a television today. (v) Arif has already eaten four idlis at breakfast; his willingness to pay for a fifth idli.
questions.a: (i) Income of the consumer; demand rises. (ii) Price of a related good (tea and coffee are substitutes); demand for coffee rises. (iii) Price of a related good (petrol and motorcycles are complementary); demand for motorcycles falls. (iv) Future price expectations; present demand falls as the family postpones the purchase. (v) Diminishing marginal utility; his willingness to pay falls.
s: (i) Income; rises
(ii) Substitute good; demand for coffee rises
(iii) Complementary good; demand for motorcycles falls
(iv) Future price expectations; present demand falls
(v) Diminishing marginal utility; willingness to pay falls

questions.q:
Read the case and answer the questions.
Sharma Electronics in Ludhiana sells one phone model and a pair of earphones made for it. In August the phone cost Rs 12,000 and the shop sold 50 phones and 40 earphones. In September the phone company cut the phone price to Rs 10,000; the shop sold 80 phones and 64 earphones, though the earphones stayed at Rs 800. In October a rumour spread that phone prices would fall further in November, and only 45 phones were sold.
(a) What kind of related goods are the phone and the earphones?
(b) By what percentage did earphone sales rise from August to September?
(c) Explain why earphone sales rose though their own price did not change.
(d) Which factor affecting demand explains the fall in phone sales in October?
questions.a: (a) Complementary goods, used together. (b) (64 - 40) / 40 x 100 = 60 per cent. (c) The phone became cheaper, so more phones were bought, and since earphones are used with the phone, the demand for earphones rose even at the same price. (d) Future price expectations: buyers expecting a lower price in November postponed their purchases, so present demand fell.
s: (a) Complementary goods
(b) Rise of 60 per cent, from 40 to 64
(c) Cheaper phones raised phone sales, and so the demand for the complementary earphones
(d) Future price expectations led buyers to postpone purchases

questions.q: Three marigold growers near Pune offer flowers to a wholesale market. At Rs 40 a kg, X offers 10 kg, Y 5 kg and Z nothing. At Rs 60, X offers 15 kg, Y 10 kg and Z 5 kg. At Rs 80, X offers 20 kg, Y 18 kg and Z 12 kg. (a) Find the market supply at each price. (b) By how much does market supply rise when the price goes from Rs 40 to Rs 80? (c) Which grower shows the chapter's point that higher prices attract new sellers into a market? Give a reason. (d) If X stops selling, what is the market supply at Rs 60?
questions.a: (a) Rs 40: 10 + 5 + 0 = 15 kg; Rs 60: 15 + 10 + 5 = 30 kg; Rs 80: 20 + 18 + 12 = 50 kg. (b) 50 - 15 = 35 kg. (c) Z, who offers nothing at Rs 40 and enters the market only when the price rises to Rs 60 and above. (d) 10 + 5 = 15 kg.
s: (a) Market supply 15, 30 and 50 kg
(b) Rise of 35 kg
(c) Grower Z, who enters only at higher prices
(d) 15 kg at Rs 60 without X

questions.q: A dairy cooperative in Anand collects 2,000 litres of milk a day. Without cooling, 10 per cent of it spoils before reaching the city; with a bulk milk chiller costing Rs 3,20,000, only 2 per cent would spoil. Milk sells at Rs 50 a litre. (i) How much milk reaches the city each day now, and how much would with the chiller? (ii) Which factor affecting supply does the chiller show? (iii) What would happen to the market supply of milk in the city if many cooperatives bought chillers? (iv) Using the chapter, say what is likely to happen to the price of milk for city buyers, and why. (v) The extra milk is sold at Rs 50 a litre. In how many days would the extra sales equal the cost of the chiller? Should the cooperative buy it?
questions.a: (i) Now 2,000 x 0.90 = 1,800 litres; with the chiller 2,000 x 0.98 = 1,960 litres. (ii) Technology, which reduces cost and waste so producers can supply more, like the cold storage example. (iii) Market supply would rise. (iv) When supply exceeds demand, prices fall, so city buyers may pay a lower price for milk. (v) Extra milk = 160 litres a day, worth 160 x 50 = Rs 8,000; 3,20,000 / 8,000 = 40 days. Yes: the chiller pays for itself in about 40 days and then adds to the cooperative's sales every day.
s: (i) 1,800 litres now and 1,960 litres with the chiller
(ii) Technology
(iii) Market supply rises
(iv) Price likely to fall because supply exceeds demand
(v) 160 litres worth Rs 8,000 a day, cost recovered in 40 days, so recommends buying

questions.q: In the chapter, excess demand is also called a shortage and excess supply a surplus. Explain each term in one line.
questions.a: Excess demand (shortage): at that price the quantity demanded is more than the quantity supplied (Qs < Qd). Excess supply (surplus): at that price the quantity supplied is more than the quantity demanded (Qs > Qd).
s: Excess demand or shortage: quantity demanded more than quantity supplied
Excess supply or surplus: quantity supplied more than quantity demanded

questions.q: In a market for gel pens, at Rs 5 a pen buyers want 80 pens and sellers offer 20; at Rs 10, buyers want 50 and sellers offer 50; at Rs 15, buyers want 30 and sellers offer 70. (a) How large is the excess demand at Rs 5? (b) How large is the excess supply at Rs 15? (c) What is the equilibrium quantity?
questions.a: (a) 80 - 20 = 60 pens of excess demand. (b) 70 - 30 = 40 pens of excess supply. (c) 50 pens, at Rs 10.
s: (a) Excess demand of 60 pens
(b) Excess supply of 40 pens
(c) Equilibrium quantity of 50 pens

questions.q:
Read the case and answer the questions.
Every morning, sardines are auctioned at a fish landing centre in Kochi. Traders record the quantities on a typical day. At Rs 80 a kg, buyers want 900 kg and boat owners offer 300 kg. At Rs 120 a kg, buyers want 600 kg and boat owners offer 600 kg. At Rs 160 a kg, buyers want 400 kg and boat owners offer 850 kg.
(a) What is the equilibrium price?
(b) What is the equilibrium quantity?
(c) Name the outcome at Rs 80 and give its size.
(d) Name the outcome at Rs 160 and give its size.
questions.a: (a) Rs 120 a kg, where demand equals supply. (b) 600 kg. (c) Excess demand (shortage) of 900 - 300 = 600 kg. (d) Excess supply (surplus) of 850 - 400 = 450 kg.
s: (a) Equilibrium price Rs 120
(b) Equilibrium quantity 600 kg
(c) Excess demand of 600 kg at Rs 80
(d) Excess supply of 450 kg at Rs 160

questions.q: In a town market for bananas, at Rs 30 a dozen buyers want 140 dozen and sellers offer 60; at Rs 40, 100 and 100; at Rs 50, 70 and 130. A seller says, 'Rs 50 is the best price for the market because sellers bring the most bananas at Rs 50.' Examine his claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. At Rs 50, sellers offer 130 dozen but buyers want only 70, an excess supply of 60 dozen, so many bananas stay unsold. Sellers wanting to clear stock will cut prices, so Rs 50 cannot last. The price settles at Rs 40, where demand equals supply at 100 dozen and the market is cleared, with neither shortage nor surplus.
s: Finds the excess supply of 60 dozen at Rs 50
Explains that unsold stock makes sellers lower the price
Identifies Rs 40 and 100 dozen as the equilibrium where the market clears

questions.q: In a vegetable market, the daily demand and supply of brinjal are: Rs 20 a kg, demand 900 kg, supply 300 kg; Rs 25, demand 750, supply 450; Rs 30, demand 600, supply 600; Rs 35, demand 480, supply 700; Rs 40, demand 380, supply 780. (i) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (ii) Find the excess demand at Rs 20 and at Rs 25. (iii) Find the excess supply at Rs 40. (iv) Explain how the price will move if it starts at Rs 25. (v) If all vendors insist on Rs 35, how many kilograms will remain unsold in the market each day?
questions.a: (i) Rs 30 a kg and 600 kg, where demand equals supply. (ii) Rs 20: 900 - 300 = 600 kg; Rs 25: 750 - 450 = 300 kg. (iii) 780 - 380 = 400 kg. (iv) At Rs 25 there is a shortage of 300 kg; buyers compete for the limited brinjal, so the price rises; as it rises, demand falls and supply rises until they meet at Rs 30. (v) 700 - 480 = 220 kg unsold.
s: (i) Equilibrium at Rs 30 and 600 kg
(ii) Excess demand of 600 kg at Rs 20 and 300 kg at Rs 25
(iii) Excess supply of 400 kg at Rs 40
(iv) Shortage pushes price up towards Rs 30 as demand falls and supply rises
(v) 220 kg unsold at Rs 35

questions.q: At a school fair, the lemonade stall's records show: at Rs 10 a glass, students want 260 glasses and the stall can make 80; at Rs 15, 200 and 120; at Rs 20, 160 and 160; at Rs 25, 110 and 190. The organisers keep the price at Rs 15 so that it stays 'cheap for everyone'. (a) Find the excess demand at Rs 15. (b) Name this outcome and say what students are likely to face at the stall. (c) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (d) Should the organisers move the price to Rs 20? Justify your view.
questions.a: (a) 200 - 120 = 80 glasses. (b) A shortage (excess demand): long queues, and 80 students who want lemonade go without it. (c) Rs 20 a glass, 160 glasses. (d) Either view earns the mark if it uses the data. Yes: at Rs 20 the stall makes 160 glasses and every student willing to pay Rs 20 gets one, so the market clears with no shortage, and 40 more glasses are sold than the 120 at Rs 15. No: the fair wants lemonade to be cheap, and 40 of the 200 students who would buy at Rs 15 are priced out at Rs 20 (demand falls to 160); the organisers could instead ask the stall to make more glasses at Rs 15.
s: (a) Excess demand of 80 glasses
(b) Names a shortage and its effect, such as queues and students left without lemonade
(c) Equilibrium at Rs 20 and 160 glasses
(d) A reasoned decision (either view) that uses the shortage at Rs 15 and the market clearing at Rs 20 with 160 glasses

D. Supply rises

A fishing village catches 50 per cent more fish this year by using finer nets that also trap very young fish. Analyse what this is likely to do (a) to the supply and price of fish this year, (b) to the supply of fish in later years, and (c) to the chapter's question of short-term gains versus long-term sustainability.
questions.a: (a) This year supply rises, so with supply above demand the price of fish is likely to fall. (b) Trapping young fish is overfishing: fewer fish grow and breed, so future supply falls and future prices may rise. (c) The village gains in the short term but harms its own long-term supply and income; the chapter's example shows choices today affect future resources, so sustainable fishing is wiser.
s: (a) Supply rises now, so the price is likely to fall
(b) Overfishing lowers future supply
(c) Weighs short-term gain against long-term harm, as the chapter's sustainability question asks

questions.q: A bus operator runs a 40-seat bus from Hyderabad to Vijayawada. On a weekday at Rs 600 a seat it fills 25 seats; on a Friday night at Rs 900 it fills all 40; on the eve of Sankranti at Rs 1,800 it fills all 40 and turns away 30 more passengers. (i) Find the money taken from tickets on each of the three trips. (ii) Why is the weekday fare the lowest? (iii) Is there excess demand on the Sankranti trip? Give its size. (iv) The operator tried a fixed Rs 900 fare on a weekday once and filled only 12 seats. Find his takings that day. (v) A passenger group demands one fixed fare of Rs 900 on all days. Evaluate this demand from the operator's point of view.
questions.a: (i) Weekday 600 x 25 = Rs 15,000; Friday 900 x 40 = Rs 36,000; Sankranti 1,800 x 40 = Rs 72,000. (ii) Few people travel on weekdays, so demand for seats is low and a low fare is needed to fill them. (iii) Yes, 30 passengers more than the seats available. (iv) 900 x 12 = Rs 10,800, which is Rs 4,200 less than at Rs 600. (v) A fixed fare would lose money on weekdays (Rs 10,800 instead of Rs 15,000) and on Sankranti (Rs 36,000 instead of Rs 72,000), while still leaving a shortage of seats on the festival day. Like the hotel tariffs, fares that follow demand earn more and fill seats, so the operator would reject one fixed fare, though some limit on festival fares may be fair to passengers.
s: (ii) Low weekday demand needs a low fare
(iii) Excess demand of 30 passengers
(iv) Rs 10,800 at Rs 900 on a weekday
(v) Evaluates the fixed fare using the takings and the shortage, and reaches a reasoned view

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What is hoarding? (b) What is black marketing? (c) Why do these practices make an essential good harder to get during a shortage?
questions.a: (a) Hoarding is accumulating goods beyond what is immediately needed, often from fear of shortages or to profit from expected price rises. (b) Black marketing is the illegal trade of goods and services that are banned or regulated. (c) They take goods off the open market, so supply falls further below demand, prices rise sharply and ordinary buyers cannot find or afford the good.
s: (a) Defines hoarding as stocking goods beyond immediate need
(b) Defines black marketing as illegal trade in banned or regulated goods
(c) Explains that they cut available supply and push prices up for ordinary buyers

questions.q: Neeraj says, 'The government should fix the price of every good below the market price, so that everyone can afford everything.' Examine his claim using the chapter's limitations of government intervention.
questions.a: The claim does not hold. First, prices fixed below market levels cause price distortions: producers lose the motivation to supply, so production falls and shortages follow, as in the wheat example. Second, controlling every price needs many regulations, licences and permits, a compliance burden that hurts small businesses and the ease of doing business. Third, heavy controls discourage innovation, since producers will not invest in better seeds or technology if they cannot earn adequate returns. So intervention should be careful and limited, for example to essentials in an emergency.
s: Explains price distortion: below-market prices cut supply and cause shortages
Explains the compliance burden on businesses
Explains that heavy controls discourage innovation, and concludes the claim fails

questions.q:
Read the case and answer the questions.
In a state, the market price of a pack of an essential vaccine is Rs 450. At that price, makers supply 9,000 packs a month and buyers want 9,000 packs. To make the vaccine affordable, the state fixes a maximum sale price of Rs 300 a pack. At Rs 300, buyers want 14,000 packs a month but makers supply only 6,000.
(a) What kind of price control has the state used?
(b) Find the gap between demand and supply at Rs 300 and name the outcome.
(c) Why do makers supply fewer packs at Rs 300?
(d) Give one reason, from the chapter, why the state may still have chosen to act.
questions.a: (a) A price ceiling, a maximum price, set below the market price. (b) 14,000 - 6,000 = 8,000 packs a month: a shortage (excess demand). (c) The price is below the market level, so makers earn less and lose the motivation to supply, a price distortion. (d) Essential goods like medicines must be accessible to all, so the state acts for fairness and the welfare of vulnerable and low-income groups.
s: (a) A price ceiling
(b) Shortage of 8,000 packs
(c) Lower price cuts makers' incentive to supply (price distortion)
(d) Fairness and access to essentials for low-income groups
